screens.title: NuGet and Azure Artifacts: The Foundation
screens.narratorSegment: At its heart, NuGet is the package manager for. NET, a vital tool that empowers developers to create, share, and consume reusable code. Think of it as a central hub for all your. NET libraries and components. While public sources like nuget. org are excellent for open-source packages, a DevOps environment, especially one leveraging Azure DevOps, benefits immensely from Azure Artifacts. Azure Artifacts provides a private, secure, and high-performance repository specifically for your internal NuGet packages. This means your proprietary code doesn't need to be exposed publicly. Beyond security, it also acts as a reliable cache for external dependencies, speeding up builds and ensuring consistent access even if public sources experience issues. This combination creates a robust ecosystem where your teams can efficiently manage all their code dependencies, both internal and external, from a single, trusted source. It's about bringing control, security, and performance to your dependency management strategy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 9›Chapter 9.3›NuGet & Azure Artifacts
Core Concept

NuGet and Azure Artifacts: The Foundation

Understand the synergy between .NET's package manager and Azure's private feeds.

Why Azure Artifacts for NuGet?

  • Private Repository: Host your internal libraries securely, preventing public exposure.
  • Secure Access: Control who can access and publish packages with Azure DevOps permissions.
  • Performant Cache: Cache external NuGet packages, speeding up builds and ensuring reliability.
  • Centralized Management: Manage all your .NET dependencies from a single, integrated platform.
Key Takeaway

Azure Artifacts enhances NuGet by providing a secure, private, and performant solution for managing both internal and external .NET package dependencies.

screens.title: Configuring NuGet Clients Locally
screens.narratorSegment: The first crucial step to integrating NuGet with Azure Artifacts is configuring your NuGet client to recognize and authenticate with your private feed. For local development, this primarily involves modifying the nuget. config file. This XML file acts as a central configuration point, defining your package sources and authentication details. You can either manually edit this file or use the dotnet nuget add source command, which is often more convenient. When you add a source, you'll specify a key, which is a friendly name for your feed, and the actual feed URL from Azure Artifacts. The authentication mechanism for local clients typically relies on the Azure DevOps credential provider, which intelligently handles token acquisition, making the process seamless. Without this configuration, your local dotnet CLI or Visual Studio instance won't know where to find your private packages, leading to restore failures. It's like giving your package manager a map and a key to a private library. Configuring NuGet Clients Locally means the `nuget.config` file defines package sources and authentication, enabling local clients to access private azure artifacts feeds.. In practical terms, set up your local environment to access private azure artifacts feeds.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9›Chapter 9.3›Client Configuration
Configuration

Configuring NuGet Clients Locally

Set up your local environment to access private Azure Artifacts feeds.

Key Steps for Local Configuration

  • Locate/Create `nuget.config`: This file can be in your project root, user profile, or system-wide.
  • Add Feed Source: Use `dotnet nuget add source` or manually add an entry to `packageSources`.
  • Ensure Authentication: The Azure DevOps Credential Provider handles token acquisition for seamless access.
Key Takeaway

Proper `nuget.config` setup with the correct feed URL and authentication mechanism is essential for local NuGet client interaction with Azure Artifacts.

Example: nuget.config
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?> <configuration> <packageSources> <add key="nuget.org" value="https://api.nuget.org/v3/index.json" protocolVersion="3" /> <add key="MyOrgNuGetFeed" value="https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/YourOrg/_packaging/MyOrgNuGetFeed/nuget/v3/index.json" /> </packageSources> <!-- Authentication details are often handled by credential providers --> </configuration>
Command Line Example
dotnet nuget add source "https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/YourOrg/_packaging/MyOrgNuGetFeed/nuget/v3/index.json" --name "MyOrgNuGetFeed"

screens.title: Secure Authentication for Local Clients
screens.narratorSegment: While the nuget. config file defines your package sources, secure authentication is paramount when accessing private feeds. For local development, the Azure Artifacts Credential Provider is the recommended and most secure method. This provider integrates with Visual Studio and the. NET CLI, automatically handling the acquisition and refreshing of authentication tokens, so you don't have to manage Personal Access Tokens, or PATs, directly. It leverages your existing Azure DevOps login, providing a seamless and secure experience. However, if the credential provider isn't an option, or for specific automation scenarios, you might consider using a PAT. It's crucial to understand that storing PATs directly in nuget. config is generally discouraged for shared environments due to security risks. If you must use a PAT, ensure it has the minimum necessary scope, such as 'Packaging (read)', and consider environment variables or secure configuration management tools to avoid hardcoding it. Always prioritize the credential provider for its enhanced security and ease of use. Module 9›Chapter 9.3›Secure Authentication
Security Best Practice

Secure Authentication for Local Clients

Understand credential providers and safe PAT usage for private feeds.

Credential Provider

Automatically handles token acquisition and refresh, leveraging your Azure DevOps login. Recommended for Visual Studio and .NET CLI.

Personal Access Token (PAT)

A static token for authentication. Use with caution; avoid hardcoding in `nuget.config` for shared environments.

Safety Note

Storing PATs directly in `nuget.config` is discouraged. Use the Azure Artifacts Credential Provider or secure environment variables instead.

Key Takeaway

Prioritize the Azure Artifacts Credential Provider for local authentication due to its superior security and ease of management over manual PATs.

Authentication Flow

Credential Provider
1

.NET CLI / VS requests package

2

Credential Provider intercepts request

3

Authenticates with Azure DevOps

4

Provides token to NuGet client

screens.title: Configuring NuGet in Azure Pipelines
screens.narratorSegment: While local development uses credential providers, Azure Pipelines streamline NuGet configuration using dedicated tasks. Within your CI/CD pipelines, you don't manually edit nuget. config or manage PATs for the build agent. Instead, tasks like Nu Get Authenticate@1 or Dot Net Core CLI@2 automatically handle the setup. These tasks configure the build agent's NuGet environment to work seamlessly with your Azure Artifacts feeds. They leverage the pipeline's service identity for authentication, which is a secure and managed way to grant access. This means your pipeline's service principal, which is automatically created and managed by Azure DevOps, will be used to authenticate against your private feeds. This approach eliminates the need to embed sensitive credentials directly into your pipeline YAML or manage them separately, significantly enhancing security and simplifying pipeline maintenance. It's a powerful abstraction that ensures your builds can always access the necessary packages without manual intervention. Configuring NuGet in Azure Pipelines means azure pipelines tasks like `dotnetcorecli@2` automatically configure nuget and use the pipeline's service identity for secure authentication to azure artifacts feeds.. In practical terms, streamline nuget feed access for your automated builds.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9›Chapter 9.3›Pipeline Configuration
Pipeline Integration

Configuring NuGet in Azure Pipelines

Streamline NuGet feed access for your automated builds.

How Pipelines Authenticate

  • Dedicated Tasks: Use `NuGetAuthenticate@1` or `DotNetCoreCLI@2` to configure the build agent.
  • Service Identity: Authentication uses the pipeline's service identity, not personal credentials.
  • Secure & Automated: Eliminates manual `nuget.config` editing and PAT management in pipelines.
Key Takeaway

Azure Pipelines tasks simplify NuGet configuration and securely authenticate to Azure Artifacts feeds using the pipeline's service identity, ensuring smooth automated builds.

Example: Pipeline Task
steps: - task: DotNetCoreCLI@2 displayName: 'Restore dependencies' inputs: command: 'restore' projects: '**/*.csproj' feedsToUse: 'config' # Uses nuget.config for sources # Alternatively, specify feed directly: # feedsToUse: 'select' # nugetFeedType: 'internal' # feedRestore: 'MyOrgNuGetFeed'
Common Mistake

Forgetting to grant the pipeline's build service identity 'Reader' permissions on the Azure Artifacts feed will lead to authentication failures during restore.

Module 9›Chapter 9.3›Publishing Overview
Publishing Process

Publishing NuGet Packages: Overview

Learn the fundamental steps to share your internal .NET libraries.

The Two-Step Publishing Flow

  • 1. Create the Package (`dotnet pack`): Generates the `.nupkg` file containing your compiled code and metadata.
  • 2. Publish the Package (`dotnet nuget push`): Uploads the `.nupkg` file to your designated Azure Artifacts feed.
Key Takeaway

The `dotnet pack` and `dotnet nuget push` commands are the core tools for publishing your .NET libraries as NuGet packages to Azure Artifacts, typically within a CI pipeline.

Publishing Flow

CI Pipeline

Build .NET Project

2

Run Tests

3

`dotnet pack` (Create .nupkg)

4

`dotnet nuget push` (Publish to Feed)

Walk through the Azure Pipeline steps for preparing your NuGet package.

Key Tasks Explained

  • `dotnet restore`: Downloads all project dependencies from configured NuGet feeds.
  • `dotnet build`: Compiles the .NET project into executable assemblies.
  • `dotnet pack`: Creates the `.nupkg` file, placing it in `$(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)`.
Key Takeaway

The `restore`, `build`, and `pack` tasks in an Azure Pipeline are sequential steps to prepare a .NET library for publishing as a NuGet package.

Example: Pipeline YAML Snippet
steps: - task: DotNetCoreCLI@2 displayName: 'Restore dependencies' inputs: command: 'restore' projects: '**/*.csproj' - task: DotNetCoreCLI@2 displayName: 'Build project' inputs: command: 'build' projects: '**/*.csproj' arguments: '--configuration $(buildConfiguration)' - task: DotNetCoreCLI@2 displayName: 'Pack NuGet package' inputs: command: 'pack' projects: '**/MyLibrary.csproj' arguments: '--configuration $(buildConfiguration) --output "$(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)"'
Common Mistake

Incorrectly specifying the `projects` path for the `pack` task can lead to the `.nupkg` file not being generated or the wrong project being packaged.

Module 9›Chapter 9.3›Pipeline Push
Pipeline YAML

Publishing NuGet Packages: Push & Troubleshooting

Finalize package publication and address common issues.

Key Considerations for `dotnet nuget push`

  • Feed Configuration: Ensure `nuGetFeedType` and `publishVstsFeed` are correctly set.
  • Permissions: Pipeline's build identity needs 'Contributor' role on the target feed.
  • `allowPackageConflicts`: Useful for pre-release versions to overwrite existing packages.
Key Takeaway

Successful package publishing requires precise feed configuration and appropriate 'Contributor' permissions for the pipeline's build identity on the Azure Artifacts feed.

Example: Publish Task
- task: DotNetCoreCLI@2 displayName: 'Publish NuGet package to Azure Artifacts' inputs: command: 'push' packagesToPush: '$(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)/*.nupkg' nuGetFeedType: 'internal' publishVstsFeed: '$(nugetPackageFeed)' # Or '$(nugetPackageProject)/$(nugetPackageFeed)' allowPackageConflicts: true
Common Mistake

A '403 Forbidden' error during `push` indicates the pipeline's build identity lacks 'Contributor' permissions on the target Azure Artifacts feed.

Module 9›Chapter 9.3›Package Consumption
Consumption

Consuming NuGet Packages: Project Reference

Integrate private NuGet packages into your .NET projects.

How to Reference a Package

  • Add `PackageReference`: Include an `ItemGroup` with `PackageReference` in your `.csproj` file.
  • Specify Package Name & Version: Use the exact name and desired version of your NuGet package.
  • Run `dotnet restore`: This command resolves and downloads the package from your configured feeds.
Key Takeaway

Consuming NuGet packages from Azure Artifacts is done via `PackageReference` in the `.csproj` file, relying on `dotnet restore` to resolve dependencies from configured feeds.

Example: .csproj Reference
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web"> <PropertyGroup> <TargetFramework>net8.0</TargetFramework> </PropertyGroup> <ItemGroup> <PackageReference Include="MyOrg.MyLibrary" Version="1.0.0" /> <!-- Your internal package --> <PackageReference Include="Newtonsoft.Json" Version="13.0.3" /> <!-- Public package (cached) --> </ItemGroup> </Project>
Common Mistake

Forgetting to configure `nuget.config` with your Azure Artifacts feed will prevent `dotnet restore` from finding your private packages.

screens.title: Implementing Versioning Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Versioning strategy is absolutely crucial for managing NuGet packages effectively, especially in a collaborative environment. Semantic Versioning, or SemVer, is the industry standard, using a MAJOR. MINOR. PATCH format, like 1.2.3. This scheme conveys clear meaning: a major version increment indicates breaking changes, a minor version for new features that are backward-compatible, and a patch for backward-compatible bug fixes. For pre-release versions, you can append a label, such as 1.2.3-beta.1. In Azure Pipelines, you can automate versioning to ensure consistency. For instance, you might use 1.0.$ open parenthesis Build. Build Id close parenthesis for pre-release builds, where Build. Build Id is a unique identifier for each pipeline run. For official releases, you would manually increment the MAJOR. MINOR. PATCH components. This automation ensures traceability, allowing you to link a specific package version back to the exact build that produced it. Azure Artifacts fully supports multiple versions of the same package, giving consumers the flexibility to choose the specific version they need, which is vital for managing dependencies and avoiding unexpected breaking changes. content.html:
Module 9›Chapter 9.3›Versioning Strategy
Best Practice

Implementing Versioning Strategies

Ensure consistency and traceability for your NuGet packages.

Semantic Versioning (SemVer)

  • MAJOR: Breaking changes (e.g., `1.0.0` to `2.0.0`).
  • MINOR: New features, backward-compatible (e.g., `1.0.0` to `1.1.0`).
  • PATCH: Bug fixes, backward-compatible (e.g., `1.0.0` to `1.0.1`).
  • Pre-release: Appended label (e.g., `1.0.0-beta.1`).
Key Takeaway

Adopting Semantic Versioning and automating versioning in pipelines ensures clear package stability, traceability, and controlled dependency management.

Automated Versioning

Azure Pipelines
1

Use `versioningScheme: 'byBuildNumber'`

2

Set `versionMajor` and `versionMinor`

3

Patch version becomes `$(Build.BuildNumber)`

4

Example: `1.0.$(Build.BuildId)`

screens.title: Common Issue: NuGet Feed Not Found
screens.narratorSegment: Encountering a 'NuGet feed not found' error during dotnet restore is a common hurdle, but it's usually straightforward to troubleshoot. The most frequent culprit is an incorrect nuget. config configuration. This means the nuget. config file, whether it's in your project root, user profile, or system-wide, either doesn't define your Azure Artifacts feed correctly, or the URL itself is wrong. It's like having a map with a missing or incorrect address. You should always verify the key attribute matches your feed name exactly and that the value attribute points to the precise Azure Artifacts feed URL. Another significant reason for this error is an authentication failure. Even if the feed is listed correctly, dotnet restore might lack the necessary credentials to access a private feed. For local development, ensure the Azure Artifacts Credential Provider is installed and configured. If using a Personal Access Token, double-check its configuration in nuget. config and confirm it has the 'Packaging (read)' scope. In pipelines, verify that the build service identity has at least 'Reader' permissions on the feed. Addressing these points will typically resolve the 'feed not found' issue.

Module 9›Chapter 9.3›Troubleshooting
Troubleshooting

Common Issue: NuGet Feed Not Found

Diagnose and resolve errors when `dotnet restore` can't find your feed.

Root Causes & Solutions

  • Incorrect `nuget.config`: The feed URL or name is misspelled or missing.
    Solution: Verify `nuget.config` for exact feed name and URL. Use "Connect to feed" in Azure Artifacts for the correct URL.
  • Authentication Failure: Lack of credentials to access the private feed.
    Solution: Install Azure Artifacts Credential Provider (local) or ensure pipeline identity has 'Reader' permissions (pipeline).
Key Takeaway

When a NuGet feed is not found, always check your `nuget.config` for correct feed details and verify that the client or pipeline has proper authentication to access the private feed.

Troubleshooting Flow

Feed Not Found
1

Check `nuget.config` for feed URL & name

2

Verify Azure Artifacts Credential Provider (local)

3

Confirm pipeline build identity permissions

screens.title: Common Issue: 403 Forbidden Error
screens.narratorSegment: Another common and frustrating error when publishing NuGet packages to Azure Artifacts is the '403 Forbidden' error. This error message is a clear indicator that the identity attempting to push the package lacks the necessary permissions on the target feed. In the context of an Azure Pipeline, the most probable cause is insufficient permissions for the pipeline's build service identity. When a pipeline runs, it uses a service principal, often named something like open square bracket Project Name close square bracket Build Service open parenthesis open square bracket Your Org Name close square bracket close parenthesis, to interact with Azure DevOps resources, including Artifacts feeds. If this build service identity only has 'Reader' permissions, it can consume packages but cannot publish them. To resolve this, you must navigate to your Azure Artifacts feed settings, go to the 'Permissions' tab, and locate the relevant build service identity. You then need to ensure this identity has at least the 'Contributor' role on the feed. The 'Contributor' role grants the necessary rights to push packages, allowing your pipeline to successfully publish your. nupkg files. Always remember to check permissions first when you encounter a '403 Forbidden' error during publishing.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome to this chapter on managing NuGet packages with Azure Artifacts. In modern software development, efficiently sharing and reusing code is paramount, especially in a DevOps environment. NuGet, the package manager for. NET, is your primary tool for this. When combined with Azure Artifacts, it provides a robust, private, and secure repository for your internal libraries, while also offering a reliable cache for external dependencies. This integration streamlines your development process, enhances security by controlling package sources, and ensures consistency across your projects. Over the next few screens, we'll explore how to configure your development environment and Azure Pipelines to seamlessly work with Azure Artifacts, enabling you to publish your own packages and consume others with confidence. You'll learn the practical steps to integrate these powerful tools into your daily workflow, making your software delivery more efficient and reliable.

Our journey through managing NuGet packages with Azure Artifacts will equip you with several key competencies. First, you'll learn how to configure your NuGet clients, whether for local development or within Azure Pipelines, to securely authenticate and interact with your private Azure Artifacts feeds. This is foundational, as it establishes the trust relationship between your development environment and your package repository. You'll understand the nuances of nuget. config and the role of credential providers. Secondly, we'll dive into the process of publishing your own NuGet packages. This involves taking your compiled. NET libraries and making them available for others to consume, typically as part of a Continuous Integration pipeline. You'll see how to use dotnet pack to create the package and dotnet nuget push to publish it, ensuring your internal components are easily shareable and version-controlled. These skills are vital for fostering code reuse and maintaining a consistent component library across your organization.

Continuing our learning objectives, you will also gain proficiency in consuming NuGet packages from your Azure Artifacts feed within your. NET projects. This is the other side of the coin: once packages are published, you need to know how to integrate them into your applications, leveraging the shared code. You'll understand how Package Reference works in your project files and how dotnet restore resolves these dependencies. Furthermore, we'll delve into implementing effective versioning strategies for your NuGet packages. Consistent and traceable versioning, often following Semantic Versioning principles, is critical for managing updates, preventing breaking changes, and ensuring that consumers always get the correct package stability. Finally, you'll learn to troubleshoot common issues that arise when working with NuGet and Azure Artifacts, such as authentication failures or incorrect feed configurations. This practical problem-solving ability will solidify your understanding and make you more effective in a real-world DevOps setting.

At its heart, NuGet is the package manager for. NET, a vital tool that empowers developers to create, share, and consume reusable code. Think of it as a central hub for all your. NET libraries and components. While public sources like nuget. org are excellent for open-source packages, a DevOps environment, especially one leveraging Azure DevOps, benefits immensely from Azure Artifacts. Azure Artifacts provides a private, secure, and high-performance repository specifically for your internal NuGet packages. This means your proprietary code doesn't need to be exposed publicly. Beyond security, it also acts as a reliable cache for external dependencies, speeding up builds and ensuring consistent access even if public sources experience issues. This combination creates a robust ecosystem where your teams can efficiently manage all their code dependencies, both internal and external, from a single, trusted source. It's about bringing control, security, and performance to your dependency management strategy. NuGet and Azure Artifacts: The Foundation means azure artifacts offers a private, secure, and performant repository for internal nuget packages and a reliable cache for external dependencies.. In practical terms, understand the synergy between .net's package manager and azure's private feeds.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The first crucial step to integrating NuGet with Azure Artifacts is configuring your NuGet client to recognize and authenticate with your private feed. For local development, this primarily involves modifying the nuget. config file. This XML file acts as a central configuration point, defining your package sources and authentication details. You can either manually edit this file or use the dotnet nuget add source command, which is often more convenient. When you add a source, you'll specify a key, which is a friendly name for your feed, and the actual feed URL from Azure Artifacts. The authentication mechanism for local clients typically relies on the Azure DevOps credential provider, which intelligently handles token acquisition, making the process seamless. Encountering a 'NuGet feed not found' error during dotnet restore is a common hurdle, but it's usually straightforward to troubleshoot. The most frequent culprit is an incorrect nuget. config configuration. This means the nuget. config file, whether it's in your project root, user profile, or system-wide, either doesn't define your Azure Artifacts feed correctly, or the URL itself is wrong. It's like having a map with a missing or incorrect address. You should always verify the key attribute matches your feed name exactly and that the value attribute points to the precise Azure Artifacts feed URL. Another significant reason for this error is an authentication failure. Even if the feed is listed correctly, dotnet restore might lack the necessary credentials to access a private feed. For local development, ensure the Azure Artifacts Credential Provider is installed and configured. If using a Personal Access Token, double-check its configuration in nuget. config and confirm it has the 'Packaging (read)' scope. In pipelines, verify that the build service identity has at least 'Reader' permissions on the feed. Addressing these points will typically resolve the 'feed not found' issue.

Another common and frustrating error when publishing NuGet packages to Azure Artifacts is the '403 Forbidden' error. This error message is a clear indicator that the identity attempting to push the package lacks the necessary permissions on the target feed. In the context of an Azure Pipeline, the most probable cause is insufficient permissions for the pipeline's build service identity. When a pipeline runs, it uses a service principal, often named something like open square bracket Project Name close square bracket Build Service open parenthesis open square bracket Your Org Name close square bracket close parenthesis, to interact with Azure DevOps resources, including Artifacts feeds. If this build service identity only has 'Reader' permissions, it can consume packages but cannot publish them. To resolve this, you must navigate to your Azure Artifacts feed settings, go to the 'Permissions' tab, and locate the relevant build service identity. You then need to ensure this identity has at least the 'Contributor' role on the feed. The 'Contributor' role grants the necessary rights to push packages, allowing your pipeline to successfully publish your. nupkg files.
